In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of male secondary sexual traits, and the way they evolve in response to sexual selection.
the development and evolution of male sexual dimorphism in insects, and in particular, the role that allometry plays in the evolution of these dimorphisms.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are many examples of positive allometry in male dimorphisms, and that the existence of reprogrammed growth trajectories is rare.
there is no single explanation of horn dimorphisms in Onthophagus.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown the importance of scale for the expression of male secondary sexual traits.
there is a continuum of phenotypic expression in these three species, and this expression is a function of the size and age of the individual, as well as the resource availability.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the developmental independence of alternative male phenotypes is not a general rule.
the developmental independence of alternative reproductive phenotypes can be a consequence of the allometry of traits rather than their developmental independence per se.
allometric modeling provides a simple, robust method to test for reprogramming in dimorphic traits.
